name: Ceramide EOP
lead: Ceramide EOP is a skin ceramide, a waxy lipid made of a sphingoid base joined to a fatty acid, that appears on ingredient lists of barrier-repair moisturisers. Ceramides in general are a component of the stratum corneum lipid matrix, where, together with cholesterol and free fatty acids, they form the water-limiting barrier of the outer skin [1].

The wiki's source base for this specific ceramide subtype is very thin. General encyclopedia coverage of ceramides describes their role in the skin barrier and their inclusion in creams, soaps and some eczema-related topical products, but does not discuss ceramide EOP by name or summarise clinical trials of moisturiser efficacy [1].

paras: Ceramides are lipids built from sphingosine and a fatty acid linked by an amide bond. In the stratum corneum they are described as the mortar between skin cells in a bricks-and-mortar model, helping limit water loss and block microbes [1]. Epidermal ceramides are grouped into classes (for example AS, NS, EOS and AP) according to their chemical structure [1].
Ceramide levels are reported to fall with dry or polluted air, harsh detergents, heat, UV exposure and ageing, and the class profile differs in conditions such as psoriasis [1].

Ceramide-containing moisturisers are marketed for dry or compromised skin, and ceramide EOP is one of several ceramide types listed in such formulas. Encyclopedia coverage notes that ceramides appear in cosmetics including skin creams and sunscreens [1].

card.summary: A skin-barrier ceramide listed in moisturisers; little is published on this subtype specifically.
card.note: Subtype-specific evidence is sparse; research is mostly on ceramides as a class.

quick.overview:
Ceramide EOP is one of the skin's own ceramides, which are lipids that help hold water in the outer skin layer. It shows up in barrier-repair moisturisers.

Published material on this particular subtype is thin, so most of what is known comes from ceramides as a group.
quick.mechanism: Ceramides sit in the lipid matrix between skin cells with cholesterol and fatty acids, forming a barrier that limits water loss.
quick.risks: It is a cosmetic ingredient. No subtype-specific safety or efficacy findings were located.
